questions.q: A factory of {w} workers makes {o} units a week. What is labour productivity, in units per worker?

questions.why: Production turns the services of factors into goods and services.

questions.q: A firm hires 10% more workers and output rises 10%. What has happened?
options: Production has risen, but labour productivity is unchanged
questions.why: Output per worker is the same, so productivity has not changed.

questions.q: Which is most likely to raise labour productivity?
options: A longer lunch break for no reason
A rise in the price of the product
Hiring more workers on the same terms
questions.why: Better skills mean more output per hour.

questions.q: Higher labour productivity can lower a firm's labour cost per unit.
questions.why: More output from the same wage bill means each unit carries less labour cost.

questions.q: Firm A has 10 workers making 500 units. Firm B has 20 workers making 800 units. Which is true?
options: Firm A has higher labour productivity
Firm B has higher labour productivity
They have the same labour productivity
questions.why: Firm A makes 50 units per worker and Firm B makes 40. B produces more in total, but A is more productive.

questions.q: What is the division of labour?
options: Splitting production into tasks, each done by a specialist worker
questions.why: Each worker concentrates on one task.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of specialisation?
options: Workers become faster and more skilled at a task
questions.why: Repetition builds speed and skill, so output rises.

questions.q: Which is a drawback of the division of labour?
questions.why: Boring, repetitive work can reduce motivation and quality.

questions.q: Barter requires a double coincidence of wants.
questions.why: Each side must want what the other has. Money removes that need.

questions.q: Why does specialisation need an efficient means of exchange?
options: Because specialists make only some of what they need, so they must trade for the rest
Because money is itself a factor of production
questions.why: Specialists depend on trading with others, and money makes that easy.

questions.q: Which is an example of regional specialisation?
options: An area that concentrates on making one product, such as a region known for pottery
A family that grows all its own food
questions.why: Specialisation can happen at the level of workers, firms, regions and countries.

questions.q: Explain why a specialised economy could not work well using barter.

ideas.label: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants, so trades are hard to arrange
Specialists rely on trade for what they don't make, and money solves this

questions.model: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants, so it takes a long time to find someone to trade with. Specialists rely on trading for everything they do not make, so they need money as a medium of exchange.
questions.why: Specialists trade a lot, and barter makes trading slow.

tests.answer: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants, so specialists who rely on trading would struggle. Money solves this.
You need a double coincidence of wants.
